task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: How to measure and attribute defensive impact on opponent's intra-game performance changes?
What metrics are suitable for 'H2-H1 change' in opponent performance?
How to assess the reliability or consistency of a team-level defensive trait?
What are common confounders in studies of defensive impact?
What statistical methods are used for analyzing team trait reliability across games/seasons?
Is the available data (play-by-play, box-score) sufficient to construct relevant metrics?
Is the sample size (120 team-seasons) adequate for reliability analysis?

historical_evidence.finding: Connector quality Q_p (teammate-initiated on-off PPP gap) is not a stable player-season attribute. Pearson r(Q_a,Q_b)=+0.215 p=0.0297; Spearman rho=+0.242. Spearman-Brown Q~0.355, S~0.278. Sign agreement 65.7% (67/102) binomial p=0.000996. ICC(player-season)=0.216 (78.4% within). Split-half r=0.215 / SB 0.355 is too low to treat Q_p as a stable scoutable trait; most variance is within-player half-to-half.

When a defense drops a play type >=0.25 PPP H1 to H2, playsheet counter ranking predicts which alternative scored better in H2 (BEST > SECOND > AVOID). Spearman rho=-0.0639, p=0.099717, n=665 (no clear full-rank signal). Kruskal-Wallis H=32.9723, p=2.7e-05. Mann-Whitney BEST 1.257 (n=56) vs AVOID 1.092 (n=160), U=5546.0, p=0.004018. Trigger accuracy rho=0.4525, n=121. The study was inconclusive with limitations including low measurement reliability and small sample.

Opponent PPP rises on the next 1-3 possessions after a star's 2nd personal foul in Q1/Q2. Including FT: lag-1 ATT=+0.204 CI[+0.163,+0.245] (artifact: FT share 41.8% vs 9.9%). Excluding FT: lag-1 +0.0486 [-0.0060,+0.0991] perm p=0.0655; lag-2 -0.0192; lag-3 -0.0272. No lag clears CI+perm+placebo. Raw lag-1 +0.204 (p=0.0005) was 41.8% FT vs 9.9% control. Apples-to-apples +0.049, not significant.

PCI (halfcourt PPP + second-chance - TO - transition leakage) explains Net Rating beyond ORtg, Pace, and FGA/poss. A R2=0.763 OOS 0.761; C R2=0.902 OOS 0.919; dR2=+0.139. Offensive-control components add +0.005 R2 beyond ORtg. Net~ORtg+leakage R2=0.948. corr(leakage, DRtg)=+0.894. PCI univariate r=+0.863 vs ORtg +0.866. Headline PCI gain is leakage tracking DRtg (+0.89); offensive-control dR2=+0.005. Baseline omitted defense by construction (Net=ORtg-DRtg).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attempting to establish 'Connector teammate-path quality Q_p' as a stable player-season attribute based on split-half reliability.
failed_approaches.why: A_unanswerable (question not answerable with the data or design), [prior work]. Split-half r=0.215 / SB 0.355 was too low; most variance was within-player half-to-half.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Validating ranked playsheets by observing H1 to H2 changes in play type PPP against a defense.
failed_approaches.why: E_unclear (mechanism unclear from [prior work]), [prior work], [prior work], [prior work]. No clear full-rank signal was found.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Measuring opponent PPP rise after a star's 2nd personal foul in Q1/Q2 without accounting for free throws.
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact (apparent effect produced by a construction, selection or labelling flaw), [prior work]. The initial observed effect was an artifact of including free throws, which disproportionately occurred after fouls.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using 'Possession Control Index' as a DRtg proxy to explain Net Rating, claiming incremental R2.
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact (apparent effect produced by a construction, selection or labelling flaw), [prior work]. The headline gain was leakage tracking DRtg, and the baseline omitted defense by construction.

evidence_establishes: Measuring player or team traits based on split-half performance (e.g., H1 vs H2) is highly susceptible to low measurement reliability, often with most variance being within-unit ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
Low measurement reliability can render a research question untestable if the proposed trait cannot be consistently observed above noise ([prior work][prior work]).

Studies involving intra-game performance changes and defensive impact are prone to methodological risks such as confounding, leakage, and artifacts ([prior work][prior work], FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
Careful consideration of metric construction is necessary to avoid artifacts, such as those caused by neglecting free throws (FAM:[prior work]) or leakage ([prior work][prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the specific metric 'a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change' will or will not demonstrate sufficient reliability to be considered a stable team trait.
The precise magnitude of measurement reliability for the proposed 'H2-H1 change' metric.
Whether a specifically designed and carefully controlled methodology could overcome potential reliability issues for this particular trait.
own_inferences: The core challenge for this research question will be demonstrating that the H2-H1 change in opponent performance against a defense is a sufficiently stable and consistent signal to be considered a 'reliable team trait,' rather than predominantly random variation or game-specific noise.
The definition of 'effect on opponents' H2-H1 change' needs to be precisely operationalized, considering potential confounders and different offensive metrics (e.g., PPP, eFG%).

The available data (120 team-seasons) is the same sample size as one study that found an artifact ([prior work][prior work]), suggesting it's sufficient for some analyses, but may still be insufficient if the signal-to-noise ratio is very low, as indicated by reliability concerns.
uncertainties: The specific metric to quantify 'H2-H1 change' in opponent performance is not defined in the research question, leaving open various interpretations (e.g., raw PPP difference, adjusted PPP, eFG%).
The precise methodology for calculating and assessing the reliability of this team trait (e.g., which statistical method for reliability, what threshold for 'reliable') is not specified.
The extent to which confounding factors (e.g., opponent quality, game situation, coaching decisions) can be controlled or accounted for in the H2-H1 change metric itself.

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence, particularly [prior work][prior work] and [prior work][prior work], significantly increased the perceived risk of low measurement reliability. This evidence directly addresses the 'reliability' aspect of the research question and suggests that similar split-half measures often fail to demonstrate sufficient stability to be considered reliable traits. This shifts the decision from a potential 'proceed' to 'proceed_with_changes' to explicitly prioritize and pre-register a comprehensive reliability assessment as the primary, and potentially only, output of the study, rather than assuming reliability and moving to inferential analysis of the trait itself. It also highlighted the need for careful metric construction to avoid artifacts.

blocking_constraints.text: Historical evidence strongly suggests that split-half measures of performance (like H2-H1 changes) often exhibit very low reliability, with most variance being within-unit noise. If this holds for the proposed trait, it cannot be considered 'reliable', making the question untestable in its affirmative sense or resulting in a rejection of the hypothesis of reliability.

Numerous factors (coach adjustments, game flow, opponent quality, foul trouble, substitutions) can confound H2-H1 performance differences, making it challenging to isolate a defense's intrinsic 'trait' effect reliably.

prior_work.summary: No prior work directly answered whether 'a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait'. However, [prior work][prior work] found that a player-season split-half metric had very low reliability, rendering it untestable as a stable trait. [prior work][prior work], which also looked at H1 to H2 changes for defenses against play types, noted low measurement reliability as a limitation. These findings suggest a significant challenge in establishing reliability for such intra-game differential metrics.

risks.text: The primary risk is that the 'H2-H1 change' in opponent performance against a defense will exhibit very low reliability across games or within seasons, meaning the signal-to-noise ratio is too low for it to be considered a stable 'team trait'. Historical evidence ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]) indicates this is a high probability for split-half performance metrics.

H2-H1 changes in opponent performance can be influenced by numerous factors beyond a defense's inherent 'trait', such as opponent coaching adjustments, game situation (score, clock), fatigue, foul trouble (FAM:[prior work]), and specific matchups. It will be challenging to isolate the defensive trait from these confounders.

While 120 team-seasons are available, if the underlying reliability is very low (as suggested by historical evidence), this sample size might be insufficient to detect a statistically significant and practically meaningful level of reliability for the trait, or to distinguish a weak signal from noise.

The 'H2-H1 change' is a derived metric. Its construction (e.g., what offensive metric to use, how to normalize or adjust) can significantly impact its variability and potential reliability. Poor construction could lead to a noisy or biased metric.

Team defensive strategies, personnel, and effectiveness can evolve over a season or across seasons. What might appear as an H2-H1 'trait' early in a season might not hold late, or year-to-year, impacting reliability assessments if not accounted for.

design.estimand: The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) and Pearson split-half correlation (Spearman-Brown corrected) of a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change in points per possession (PPP) across games within a season, and across seasons for the same team.
design.unit: Team-season for reliability assessment. The base unit for computing H1 and H2 performance will be individual games.
design.sample: All available team-seasons (n=120) from 2022-23 to 2025-26. For within-season reliability, each team-season will be treated as a unit, calculating H1 and H2 PPP allowed for each game. For across-season reliability, teams with multiple seasons in the dataset will be used.
design.power: A power analysis will be conducted to determine the minimum detectable ICC and split-half correlation given the sample size of 120 team-seasons (approximately 30 teams * 4 seasons, but subject to specific team-season availability and filter criteria). The study will report the observed reliability metrics and their confidence intervals regardless of significance. A target ICC of >=0.6 or Spearman-Brown corrected r >=0.7 would be considered sufficient for a 'reliable trait'.
design.controls: To calculate 'H2-H1 change', we will define the metric as (Opponent PPP in H2 - Opponent PPP in H1) for each game. PPP will be calculated as points scored / possessions. Possessions will be adjusted for free throws (e.g., 0.44 * FTM) and turnovers. To control for opponent strength and game effects, a hierarchical model could be considered, or the H2-H1 difference will be calculated as a residual after regressing out game-level factors (e.g., opponent strength, score differential at half). Initial analysis will use raw PPP difference. Further controls for pace, substitution patterns, and foul trouble will be explored if initial reliability is low.
design.falsification: The primary falsification test is whether the calculated reliability metrics (ICC, split-half correlation) are statistically significantly greater than zero and meet a pre-defined threshold for 'reliability' (e.g., ICC >= 0.6). If the reliability metrics are low (e.g., ICC < 0.35, similar to [prior work][prior work]), the hypothesis that it is a 'reliable team trait' will be rejected.
design.multiplicity: Only one primary estimand (ICC or split-half correlation) will be used for the overall reliability assessment. Secondary analyses (e.g., different definitions of H2-H1 change, different forms of reliability) will be clearly labeled as exploratory and adjusted for multiplicity if formal hypothesis testing is performed on them.
design.decision_rule: The question will be considered 'supported' if the primary reliability metric (e.g., ICC) for the defense's H2-H1 change on opponent PPP is statistically significant (p < 0.05) and exceeds a pre-defined threshold (e.g., ICC >= 0.6). If significant but below threshold (e.g., 0.35 <= ICC < 0.6), it will be 'inconclusive'. If not significant or very low (ICC < 0.35), it will be 'rejected' as a reliable trait. The study will first focus on establishing this reliability before any further analysis of the trait itself.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs, NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs, NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs, NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13), NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21). All data will be sourced from per-game files from the NBA stats API and derived play-type possession records.
